draft_doc.title: Investment incentives and embodied carbon: should West African investment promotion agencies screen foreign direct investment by consumption-based emissions?
draft_doc.authors: Mensah, K.¹, Diallo, F.², Okonkwo, R.¹  ·  ¹ Centre for Development Policy, Fake Gulf of Guinea University  ·  ² Institute of Applied Economics, Fake Sahel University. Corresponding author: K. Mensah.
draft_doc.abstract: Background: Governments in West Africa compete for foreign direct investment with tax holidays, duty waivers and land concessions, and several of them now ask whether these incentives should be tied to the carbon footprint of the investment. Two kinds of test are discussed: a territorial test, which looks at the emissions of the plant in the host country, and a consumption-based test, which also counts the carbon embodied in imported inputs and in the goods the investor sells. Methods: We reviewed the investment codes, incentive regulations and approval guidelines of fifteen West African states in force on 30 June 2026, coded which environmental conditions each attaches to incentives, and interviewed twenty-two officials of investment promotion agencies and environment ministries. Results: Eleven of the fifteen codes attach some environmental condition to incentives, but only two refer to emissions at all, and none counts embodied carbon. Officials saw a consumption-based test as costly to administer and doubted that it was needed. Conclusions: We set out what a consumption-based test would require and weigh it against the regional evidence on foreign investment and emissions. We recommend that agencies strengthen territorial emission conditions before adding an embodied-carbon test.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Foreign direct investment is one of the main sources of private capital for West African economies, and attracting it is a stated goal of almost every national development plan in the region [1]. Investment promotion agencies offer a familiar set of instruments: corporate income tax holidays of five to fifteen years, exemptions from import duties on capital goods and raw materials, reduced rates of value added tax, guaranteed access to serviced land in industrial zones, and fast-track approval of work permits for expatriate staff [2]. These incentives are costly. Estimates of revenue forgone through investment incentives in the region range from a fraction of one percent to more than two percent of gross domestic product a year, and evaluations repeatedly find that a large share of incentivised projects would have gone ahead without them [3].
At the same time, the region's governments have made climate commitments that sit uneasily with incentives granted without regard to emissions. Most nationally determined contributions submitted by West African states include conditional targets for industrial and energy emissions, and several name foreign investment as a channel for cleaner technology [4]. The question that follows is whether incentives should be conditioned on the carbon performance of the investment, and if so, how that performance should be measured.
The measurement question matters because emissions can be counted in more than one way. Territorial or production-based accounts assign emissions to the country where the fuel is burned or the process takes place. Consumption-based accounts reassign the carbon embodied in traded goods to the country where they are finally consumed, so that a country importing carbon-intensive inputs carries their emissions, and a country exporting carbon-intensive goods passes part of its emissions on [5]. An investor can lower a host country's territorial emissions while raising its consumption-based footprint, for example by assembling locally from imported components whose production was carbon intensive, or by expanding sales of imported fuels and vehicles [6].
In recent policy discussions in the region, officials and development partners have floated the idea of a consumption-based test for incentive approvals, under which an investor would have to show that the project does not raise the embodied carbon of the host economy's consumption. Supporters argue that a territorial test alone invites the relocation of emissions to supply chains abroad and lets investors claim credit for clean plants that rely on dirty inputs. Opponents argue that the data needed for such a test do not exist at the level of a single project, that small agencies cannot administer it, and that it would deter investment for little environmental gain.
This paper contributes to that discussion in three ways. First, we document the environmental conditions that West African investment codes currently attach to incentives, which to our knowledge has not been done across the region. Second, we report what officials responsible for incentive approvals think of a consumption-based test and what they see as the obstacles. Third, we weigh the case for such a test against the evidence on how foreign investment relates to emissions in the region, and set out a recommendation for the order in which agencies should strengthen their conditions. The paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews the evidence on foreign investment, trade and emissions. Section 3 describes our documentary review and interviews. Section 4 reports what we found. Section 5 discusses the implications for the design of incentive conditions, and Section 6 concludes.

sections.heading: 2. Background: foreign investment, trade and emissions
sections.text:
Two broad expectations run through the literature on foreign investment and the environment. The first is that investors from countries with strict regulation move their most polluting activities to countries with weaker rules, so that foreign investment raises host-country emissions. The second is that foreign investors bring newer equipment, better management and access to cleaner technology, so that foreign investment lowers emissions relative to what domestic firms would emit for the same output [7]. Which effect dominates is an empirical question, and the answer appears to depend on the sector, the source country and the host country's institutions [8].
For developing regions, the evidence is mixed. Studies of manufacturing plants in coastal West Africa find that foreign-owned plants use less energy per unit of output than domestic plants in the same industry, but that their entry is followed by an expansion of output large enough to raise total sectoral emissions [9]. Country panels covering lower-income economies report both positive and negative long-run associations between foreign investment inflows and carbon emissions, and the sign often changes with the estimator and with the treatment of common shocks across countries [10, 11].
The evidence on trade is less divided. Openness to trade is predominantly emission-increasing in panel estimates for Sub-Saharan Africa covering 1990 to 2019 that use both production-based and consumption-based emissions as outcomes [14], in line with country studies that attribute rising emissions to the growth of transport and of imported fuel use [12, 13]. For incentive design, this means that projects whose business model rests on expanding imports and exports deserve particular attention, whatever the ownership of the firm.
A smaller literature compares the two ways of counting emissions directly. Consumption-based accounts for African economies are built from multi-region input-output tables, which are available for only a handful of countries at a fine sectoral level and are updated with a lag of several years [15]. Estimates for the region suggest that consumption-based emissions exceed production-based emissions in most importing economies and fall short of them in the main exporters of oil and minerals [16]. How foreign investment moves the gap between the two accounts has received little attention, which is the gap our policy question falls into.

sections.heading: 3. Data and approach
sections.text:
We reviewed the legal instruments governing investment incentives in the fifteen member states of the regional economic community: investment codes, finance acts that set incentive rates, the regulations of special economic zones, and the published approval guidelines of investment promotion agencies. We used the versions in force on 30 June 2026, obtained from official gazettes and agency websites and, where these were not available online, from the agencies directly. In total we reviewed 63 instruments.
For each state, two of us independently coded whether incentives were subject to any environmental condition, and if so, of which kind: a general obligation to comply with environmental law, a requirement for an approved environmental impact assessment before incentives are granted, a condition referring to energy efficiency or emissions, or a condition referring to emissions outside the host country. Disagreements, which concerned four of the fifteen states, were resolved by discussion with the third author.
Between March and July 2026 we interviewed twenty-two officials: fourteen from investment promotion agencies and eight from environment ministries or environmental protection agencies, in nine of the fifteen states. Interviews followed a topic guide covering the approval process for incentives, the environmental information collected from investors, the officials' views on a consumption-based test, and the capacity of their institutions to administer it. Interviews lasted between forty and seventy-five minutes, were conducted in English or French, and were recorded with consent and transcribed. We coded the transcripts thematically, starting from the topics of the guide and adding codes as new themes emerged.
The review describes rules as written, not as applied, and the interviews reflect the views of officials who agreed to take part. We return to these limitations in Section 5.

sections.heading: 4. Findings
sections.text:
Table 1 summarises the environmental conditions attached to incentives. Eleven of the fifteen investment codes attach some environmental condition to incentives, most often a requirement that the investor hold an approved environmental impact assessment before incentives are granted. Only two codes refer to energy efficiency or emissions, in both cases as one criterion among several for a higher tier of incentives, without a quantitative threshold. None refers to emissions outside the host country or to the carbon embodied in inputs or products.
Officials described the approval process as driven by employment, export earnings and the size of the investment. Environmental information is collected mainly through the impact assessment, which covers local pollution, land use and water, and rarely reports greenhouse-gas emissions. Several officials from investment promotion agencies said that their agencies had no staff with training in emissions accounting, and that they would depend on the environment ministry, whose officials in turn described long backlogs in reviewing impact assessments.
Asked about a consumption-based test, most officials were sceptical. Seventeen of the twenty-two said that the data an investor would need to show the embodied carbon of its inputs and sales could not be verified by their institution. Twelve said that such a test would put their country at a disadvantage against neighbours that did not adopt it. A minority, mostly in environment ministries, said that a territorial test alone would let investors present plants as clean while importing carbon-intensive components, and that the region should at least begin to collect the information needed for a consumption-based view.
Officials in both kinds of institution were more open to strengthening territorial conditions: requiring impact assessments to report expected annual emissions, setting energy-efficiency benchmarks for the sectors that receive most incentives, and linking the duration of tax holidays to the adoption of cleaner equipment. Eight said that these steps could be taken within existing law.

sections.heading: 5. Discussion
sections.text:
The review shows that a consumption-based test would start from almost nothing: no code in the region conditions incentives on emissions in a measurable way, and the institutions that approve incentives lack the data and staff to count embodied carbon. Building that capacity would take years and would compete for scarce staff with the more basic task of making impact assessments report emissions at all. This alone does not settle whether a consumption-based test is worth pursuing; it could still be the right long-term goal if foreign investment in the region tends to raise the carbon embodied in consumption.
The strongest reason to doubt that such a test is needed comes from the regional panel evidence. Qamruzzaman et al. [14] found that FDI is generally associated with lower production-based and consumption-based emissions in the symmetric long-run estimates for Sub-Saharan Africa. If foreign investment in the region lowers emissions even when carbon is counted where goods are finally consumed, the concern that investors shift emissions into supply chains, which motivates a consumption-based test, does not apply to the region on average. Our recommendation rests on this finding: agencies should keep their screening on territorial emission conditions and should not add an embodied-carbon test to incentive approvals.
This does not mean that every foreign project is clean. Plant and sector studies find large differences in the emissions of foreign-invested firms between industries [9, 17]. A territorial test targeted at the sectors that receive most incentives, such as cement, food processing, mining services and vehicle assembly, would catch the projects most likely to raise emissions while staying within what agencies can administer.
The officials who favoured a consumption-based view raised a fair point: a territorial test cannot see emissions embodied in imported components. Without evidence that foreign investment raises embodied emissions in the region, we see this as a reason to start collecting the information, for instance by asking investors to report the origin and quantity of their main imported inputs, rather than to make approvals depend on it.
Our study has limitations. We describe rules as written and cannot say how consistently they are applied. Our interviews cover nine of the fifteen states and only officials who agreed to take part, who may be more interested in environmental policy than their colleagues. And our weighing of the case for a consumption-based test relies on regional evidence rather than on estimates for the specific sectors and countries we studied, which would need consumption-based accounts that do not yet exist at that level [15, 18].

sections.heading: 6. Conclusion
sections.text: West African investment codes attach few measurable environmental conditions to incentives, and none that count embodied carbon. Agencies should first make impact assessments report expected emissions and set sectoral efficiency benchmarks for incentivised projects, which officials see as feasible within existing law. Collecting information on imported inputs would prepare the ground for a consumption-based view, should future evidence show that foreign investment raises embodied emissions in the region [19, 20].

expected.why: RE-changes-explained.md §8, C6: F1000Research version 2 is registered in Crossref as a `new_version` (label New version) of version 1, so the pipeline raises one medium other:new_version alert whose notice DOI is version 2 and stores version 2 as a new_version document (its Crossref title, no open-access text, its PDF); there is no notice and no current copy. Version 2's "Amendments from Version 1" say "The interpretation of the empirical findings has been revised to correspond precisely with the coefficient signs reported in the tables, particularly the contrasting effects of foreign direct investment on production-based and consumption-based CO2 emissions." Version 1's abstract said "FDI is generally associated with lower production-based and consumption-based emissions in the symmetric long-run estimates"; version 2's says "FDI is associated with lower production-based emissions but higher consumption-based emissions in the principal symmetric estimates", and its results add "Thus, the FDI result for consumption-based emissions is emission-increasing and differs from the negative FDI coefficient for production-based emissions in Table 6." A new version that changes a stated conclusion is medium (rubric), not low, even though version 1's own Table 7 text already gave a positive FDI coefficient for consumption-based emissions. The trade finding is unchanged: version 2 still says "Trade openness is predominantly emission-increasing", so the Background use (supporting, with [12, 13]) is not affected. The Discussion's recommendation rests on the reversed consumption-based FDI finding (key_evidence, affected): key_evidence x medium = medium. Other revisions (the sample, education as an expenditure proxy, funding) don't touch the draft's uses.
